source.title: Mathematical contributions to the dynamics of the Josephson junctions: state of the art and open problems

accepted.question_text: Can the perturbed sine-Gordon equation ε u_xxt + u_xx − u_tt − a u_t = sin(u) − γ be studied with interface conditions imposed on the phase u(x,t) and on its normal gradient, in order to model window Josephson junctions under the influence of an external magnetic field? Here u(x,t) is the phase difference between the wave functions of the two superconductors, ε u_xxt and a u_t represent longitudinal and shunt losses, and γ is the normalized current bias. The open problem is to formulate and analyze the resulting interface problem for the phase dynamics of such window Josephson junctions.
accepted.context_brief: Interface conditions for window Josephson junctions

evidence.quote: The flux-dynamics of a Josephson junction, i.e, two layers of superconductors separated by a very thin layer of insulating material, can be described by means of Sine Gordon equation (SGE): (1.1) uxx − utt = sin u where x denotes the direction of propagation, t is time and the variable u = u(x, t) represents the difference between the phases of the wave functions of the two superconductors.

Therefore, many authors prefer to consider the so-called perturbed sine Gordon equation (PSGE): (1.2) εuxxt + uxx − utt − aut = sin u − γ. In this case, terms εuxxt and aut represent respectively the dissipative normal electron current flow along and across the junction, (longitudinal and shunt losses) while γ is the normalized current bias [2].

It would be interesting, for example, to study equation (1.2) when interface conditions for the phase (and its normal gradient) are added, connecting, in this way, with the problems of window Josephson junctions (WJJ) when the influence of an external magnetic field must be considered [52].

accepted.question_text: When ε in the perturbed sine-Gordon model ε u_xxt + u_xx − u_tt − a u_t = sin(u) − γ is nonzero, can one estimate the diffusive effects produced by the viscous third-order term ε u_xxt? The question is to quantify how this higher-order dissipative term changes the dynamics, especially in the window-Josephson-junction setting where the ε = 0 limit recovers a standard WJJ equation.

evidence.quote: Therefore, many authors prefer to consider the so-called perturbed sine Gordon equation (PSGE): (1.2) εuxxt + uxx − utt − aut = sin u − γ. In this case, terms εuxxt and aut represent respectively the dissipative normal electron current flow along and across the junction, (longitudinal and shunt losses) while γ is the normalized current bias [2].

Indeed, letting ε = 0, (1.2) exactly recalls one of the equations usually considered for (WJJ). When, on the other hand, ε is not vanishing, a viscous term, represented by the third order term, appears. So that, it would be interesting to give an estimate of the diffusive effects due to the ε-term,too.

accepted.question_text: Given the analogy between superconductive Josephson-junction equations and reaction-diffusion systems such as the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, can Robin boundary value problems be formulated and analyzed so as to obtain results relevant to biological phenomena? In this setting, the biological reaction-diffusion side includes a membrane potential u(x,t) and a recovery variable v(x,t) modeling transmembrane current, while the superconductive side is represented by third-order parabolic equations used to describe Josephson-junction phase dynamics.

evidence.quote: Then, an equivalence between the third order equation (2.10), typical of Josephson junctions, and biological phenomena has been pointed out in [29]. Indeed, let us consider the FitzHugh-Nagumo system (FHN): [30, 31]

where u(x, t) represents a membrane potential of a nerve axon at distance x and time t, and v(x, t) is a recovery variable that models the transmembrane current. This reaction-diffusion model characterizes the theory of the propagation of nerve impulses, and the connection between a third order equation like (2.10) and the (FHN) system can be realized changing the first one into the second one under continuous parameter variations [29].

Moreover, according to the analogy between superconductor equations and reaction-diffusion models, the Robin boundary problem would be considered in order to achieve results for many biological phenomena, too [53, 54].

accepted.question_text: For exponentially shaped Josephson junctions described by ε u_xxt + u_xx − u_tt − ε λ u_xt − λ u_x − a u_t = sin(u), can the asymptotic analysis of boundary perturbations that has been done for Dirichlet boundary conditions be extended to Neumann and mixed boundary conditions? The goal is to evaluate the long-time effects of boundary disturbances for these other boundary-value formulations.

evidence.quote: When one assumes g1(x) = −g2(x) = wo e−λx, where λ is a constant that, generally, is less than one, an ESJJ is obtained. Moreover, assuming that there is no bias current so that Γ(x) = 0 and ηy = 0, the equation achieved is the following (1.8) εuxxt + uxx − utt − ελuxt − λux − aut = sin u.

Besides, a priori estimates and asymptotic properties have proved that when t tends to infinity, the effect due to the initial disturbances ( h0, h1 ) is vanishing, while the effect of the non linear source is bounded for all t. Furthermore, for large t, the effects due to boundary disturbances g1, g2 are null or at least everywhere bounded.

Besides, as for analysis on asymptotic effects due to the boundary perturbations related to equation (1.8), as it has been pointed out, the Dirichlet boundary problem has already been considered in [11]. So, the evaluation could be extended to other boundary problems, such as, for instance, Neumann and mixed ones.

accepted.question_text: For more physically significant Josephson-junction models, can the existing estimates and analysis be extended to the applied-magnetic-field equation ε u_xxt + u_xx − u_tt − a u_t = sin(u) − γ − b cos(kx), and to microshort or related variants such as ε u_xxt + u_xx − u_tt − a u_t = [1 − δ(x) μ] sin(u) − γ − b cos(kx), including cases where a gap in the vacuum chamber is considered? Here b represents an applied magnetic field parallel to the dielectric barrier plane, γ is the normalized current bias, and μ is the current density associated with the microshort.

evidence.quote: In some cases, extra terms must be considered. For example in a semiannular or in a S-shaped Josephson junction, when an applied magnetic field b parallel to the plane of the dielectric barrier is considered, the dynamic equation is: (1.3) εuxxt + uxx − utt − aut = sin u − γ − b cos(kx) where the last term evaluates a transient force on the trapped fluxons and locates these ones at the centre of the junction.

Moreover, if an annular junction, also provided with a microshort, is considered, the vortex dynamics in a static magnetic field is modelled with the general perturbed sine-Gordon equation (see,f.i. [7]): (1.4) εuxxt + uxx − utt − aut = [1 − δ(x)µ] sin u − γ − b cos(kx) where µ is the current density associated with the microshort.

Of course, in order to achieve estimates for other more significant physical problems, this analysis and many other estimates could be carried out for solution of equation (1.3) and for equations like (1.4) where the presence of a gap in the vacuum chamber is considered,too [37]

accepted.question_text: For the parabolic integro-differential operator L_R u = u_t − ε u_xx + a u + b ∫_0^t e^{−β(t−τ)} u(x,τ) dτ = F(x,t,u), can the analysis currently requiring positive constants a, b, ε, and β be extended to arbitrary values of these parameters? The motivation is to include Josephson junctions that are excluded by the positivity assumptions that are valid for the analogy with exponentially shaped Josephson junctions.
accepted.context_brief: Parameter ranges for the operator L_R

evidence.quote: An equation that is able to model all these physical problems has been introduced in [32] and it is represented by the following parabolic integro-differential equation: (2.13) LR u ≡ ut − εuxx + au + b ∫0t e−β(t−τ) u(x, τ ) dτ = F(x, t, u),
More in detail, if a, b, ε, β are positive constants, r = |x| /√ε and Jn(z) denotes the Bessel function of first kind and order n, let us consider the function (3.24) K(r, t)

The analysis conducted so far required that in (2.13) constants a, b, ε, β were all positive. This can be valid if we look for an analogy with an (ESJJ), but excludes application of (2.13) to some other junctions. Therefore it would be interesting to extend the analysis of operator LR for any value of a, b, ε, β.

accepted.question_text: Can qualitative analysis be developed for Josephson-junction operators when the coefficients ε, α, and λ are not constant, including cases in which a coefficient depends on the phase, such as a = 1 − cos(u)? The motivating constant-coefficient forms include the third-order parabolic operator L = ε∂_xxt − ∂_tt + ∂_xx − α∂_t and the exponentially shaped Josephson junction equation ε u_xxt + u_xx − u_tt − ε λ u_xt − λ u_x − a u_t = sin(u); the question is to formulate and analyze corresponding nonconstant-coefficient versions.

evidence.quote: When one assumes g1(x) = −g2(x) = wo e−λx, where λ is a constant that, generally, is less than one, an ESJJ is obtained. Moreover, assuming that there is no bias current so that Γ(x) = 0 and ηy = 0, the equation achieved is the following (1.8) εuxxt + uxx − utt − ελuxt − λux − aut = sin u.

More precisely, if one denotes by L the following linear third order parabolic operator: (2.9) L = ε∂xxt − ∂tt + ∂xx − α∂t (1.1)-(1.4) and (1.8) can be expressed by means of the unique equations: (2.10) Lu = f(x, t, u).
Finally a qualitative analysis of operators should be made in case ε, α, λ were not constant( see, f.i the case a = 1 − cos u [2]).
